craven

KRAY-vun -- rhymes with 'raven'. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Craven is contemptibly cowardly; utterly lacking in courage.

History remembers the commander's craven retreat, for he fled to safety while his soldiers still held the line.

Example

When the whistle-blower finally needed allies, the senator who had privately urged her forward proved too craven to utter a single word in her defense.

That shameful failure of courage at the decisive moment is what craven condemns. Craven is far stronger than 'afraid' -- fear is human, but craven behavior is cowardice so complete that it earns contempt.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dastardly: Dastardly adds sneakiness to cowardice — a dastardly act is both wicked and underhanded, like sabotage carried out in the dark. Craven is purely about the failure of courage itself: contemptible cowardice at the moment courage was demanded, with no scheming required.

gutless: Gutless is the blunt, informal jab for having no courage at all — the word you'd hear in a locker room. Craven means the same collapse of nerve but in elevated, literary dress: the word historians and editorials choose when cowardice deserves lasting shame.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

brave: willing to face danger or difficulty

heroic: showing exceptional courage, worthy of admiration

Where it sits · how much contempt the label carries

cowardly → craven → spineless

cowardly vs. craven: Cowardly is the plain, everyday word -- craven says the same thing with far more force and contempt, the difference between noting a failure of nerve and branding it a disgrace.

spineless vs. craven: Spineless is nearly as scornful as craven but more informal: spineless mocks someone for having no backbone at all, while craven is the elevated, literary word for cowardice so complete it deserves lasting shame.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cravant-: crushed, overwhelmed, defeated (Old French cravanter 'to crush,' possibly from Latin crepare 'to crack')

Put it together: Craven likely traces to Old French cravanter, 'to crush or overwhelm.' A craven person, at the root, is someone whose spirit has been crushed -- one who surrenders to fear rather than standing firm. The exact path into English is debated, so treat this origin as probable rather than certain.

Use the root in a new word: cravenly: The knight who fled the battlefield was said to have acted cravenly while his companions fought on.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Craven is an elevated, literary word of condemnation -- editorials, historians, and orators reach for it when 'cowardly' is not scathing enough. It often modifies acts and failures rather than people: a craven retreat, a craven surrender, a craven silence.
